title: AI-assisted design of synthetic gene editors - Nature Biotechnology
text:
Structure-guided rational design of CRISPR–Cas nucleases enables generation of non-natural nucleases with enhanced efficiency and specificity, but the conformational complexity of these RNA-guided nucleases presents a major challenge. Writing in Science, Petr Skopintsev and colleagues combine structural and evolution-based approaches to design active TnpB variants not found in nature.TnpB is transposon-encoded ancestor of CRISPR–Cas12 nucleases present in bacteria and archaea. The authors used an inverse-folding model, which, given a structure, predicts a sequence that is expected to fold into a particular shape. In addition, they incorporated evolutionary knowledge of critical residues for functionality of the enzyme. Phylogenetic analysis showed that the generated sequences shared only 50–60% sequence identity with natural TnpBs. Using a high-throughput bacterial screening and an AI-based domain-swapping strategy, the authors selected nine TnpBs variants — termed SynTnpBs — for further demonstration. These SynTnpBs displayed greater editing activity than natural TnpBs in bacterial, plant and human cells while maintaining comparable specificity. Cryo-electron microscopy and reversal mutagenesis of the most divergent SynTnpB revealed stabilizing hydrogen-bonding networks at the RNA–DNA interface and captured a previously unknown DNA-bound conformational state.
